content.title: Equations and inequalities: reading the graph

steps.caption: The equation 2x − 6 = 0 asks where the line y = 2x − 6 crosses the x-axis, and that crossing is the root.
Two lines that meet share one point, and that point is the solution of 2x + 1 = −x + 7.
An inequality asks where a graph is below the other: the parabola y = x^2 − 4 dips under the x-axis between its two roots.
The answer to 2x − 6 > 0 is a piece of the number line, running to the right of 3 because that is where the line is above the x-axis.

diagram.title: Where an equation and an inequality live on a graph
diagram.caption: An equation asks where two graphs are equal, and an inequality asks where one graph is above or below the other.

contrast.caption: A sign slip puts the boundary on the wrong side of zero; the boundary of 2x − 6 > 0 comes from 2x = 6, so it sits at 3, not at −3.

questions.why: The 5 is often moved across without changing its sign, which throws the answer off.
questions.rightWay: Subtract 5 from both sides, then divide by 3: 3x = 15, so x = 5.

questions.why: Adding 3 to the left side only leaves the two sides unequal.
questions.rightWay: Add 3 to both sides, then multiply by 2: x/2 = 7, so x = 14.

questions.why: The boundary 4 is often given, but x < 4 does not include 4 itself.
questions.prompt: 2x − 1 < 7. Find the largest whole number x.
questions.rightWay: Add 1 and divide by 2: x < 4, so the largest whole number is 3.

questions.why: The y-intercept −6 is often read off instead of the x-intercept.
questions.prompt: The line y = 2x − 6 is shown. Find the x-coordinate of the point where it crosses the x-axis.

questions.why: The 5 is sometimes subtracted instead of divided, which leaves x − 2 = 10.
questions.rightWay: Divide both sides by 5 first: x − 2 = 3, so x = 5.

questions.why: A term is often moved across the equals sign without changing its sign.
questions.rightWay: Subtract 2x from both sides, then add 3: 2x = 12, so x = 6.

questions.why: The y-value of the meeting point is sometimes given instead of the x-value.
questions.prompt: The lines y = 4x − 5 and y = −2x + 7 are shown. Find the x-coordinate of the point where they meet.
questions.rightWay: Set the two expressions equal: 4x − 5 = −2x + 7, so 6x = 12 and x = 2.

questions.why: The signs inside the brackets are often both made positive, which gives −2 and −3.
questions.rightWay: Two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to −5 are −2 and −3, so (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0 and x = 2 or x = 3.

questions.why: Dividing by a negative number without flipping the sign gives x ≥ −4.
questions.rightWay: Subtract 1, then divide by −2 and flip the sign: x ≤ −4.

questions.why: The boundary 3 is often given, but x < 3 stops just before 3.
questions.prompt: 3(x + 4) < 2x + 15. Find the largest whole number x.
questions.rightWay: Expand and collect: x < 3, so the largest whole number is 2.

questions.why: The numbers between −2 and 2 are often counted, but there the expression is negative.
questions.prompt: x^2 − 4 > 0 for whole numbers x from −5 to 5. Find how many whole numbers satisfy the inequality.
questions.rightWay: The parabola is above the axis outside its roots: x < −2 or x > 2, which gives 6 whole numbers from −5 to 5.

questions.why: The minus in front of the second fraction is often dropped, which gives −6 instead of +6.
questions.rightWay: Multiply every term by 6: 3(x + 1) − 2(x − 3) = 12, so x + 9 = 12 and x = 3.

questions.why: The outside region is often chosen, but there the parabola is above the x-axis.
questions.prompt: The parabola y = x^2 − 2x − 3 is shown. Find the values of x for which y < 0.
questions.rightWay: The roots are −1 and 3, and the parabola dips below the axis between them: −1 < x < 3.

questions.why: Only the x-value is often given, or the y-value is worked out from the wrong line.
questions.prompt: y = 3x − 2 and y = −2x + 8. Find the point where the two lines meet.
questions.rightWay: Set the expressions equal: x = 2, then substitute back: y = 4, so the point is (2; 4).

questions.why: The −1 in the exponent is often left out, so 27 is read as 3^(2x).
questions.rightWay: Write 27 as 3^3, then equate the exponents: 2x − 1 = 3, so x = 2.
